tldr: The authors proposed a system that directly generates support-free multi-axis toolpaths and collision-free robot motions from 'in-the-wild 3D models'—which may contain holes, self-intersections, and mixed thin-shell/solid geometries—without any manual geometry repair, leveraging a hybrid query field combining neural UDFs with a regularized generalized winding number.
hero_caption: Overview of WildFab. (a) A hybrid query field combining a neural UDF and a regularized generalized winding number (reg-GWN) is built from imperfect input models, (b) collisions with the dynamically growing printed geometry are avoided with high precision, and (c) support-free fabrication is achieved using an 8-DoF robotic arm. (d) The framework is also applicable to planar slicing for multi-color and multi-material 3D printing.
overview:
Multi-axis 3D printing is an attractive manufacturing technique. By leveraging multi-DoF mechanisms such as robotic arms to move the nozzle through space, it can significantly reduce support structures and improve mechanical strength. However, conventional systems have suffered from a critical bottleneck: they assume the input model is a completely closed solid, known as a watertight mesh.

In real-world design data, 3D scans, and topology-optimization outputs, geometries are often open-surfaced, feature a mix of thin shells and solids, or contain self-intersections—they exist 'in the wild.' Slicing these with conventional tools requires time-consuming manual mesh repair. Forcibly solidifying them often alters the intended geometry and destroys thin-shell structures.

Instead of forcibly repairing the model, the authors conceived a hybrid query representation that pairs two complementary geometric fields: a neural unsigned distance field (UDF) and a regularized generalized winding number field (reg-GWN). The UDF provides smooth spatial distance and direction queries throughout space, while the reg-GWN's gradient-magnitude ridges compensate for near-surface ambiguity in the fitted UDF, enabling extremely accurate surface localization.

Built upon this representation, support-free spatial toolpaths are rapidly generated via iterative projections. Furthermore, a coarse-to-fine collision checking algorithm is established to handle the time-varying, dynamically growing printed part. Validated across diverse models including self-intersecting surfaces, point clouds, and voxels, the system demonstrates high-precision, support-free fabrication on a robotic setup combining a 6-axis arm with a 2-axis tilt-rotary table.
contributions: Developed WildFab, an end-to-end computational framework for multi-axis 3D printing that directly handles 'models in the wild' such as imperfect meshes and point clouds without preprocessing or geometric repair.

Proposed a hybrid query field combining a neural UDF and a regularized generalized winding number (reg-GWN) that accurately localizes surface boundaries even on non-watertight and open-surface models.

Implemented a high-precision spatial toolpath generation method that avoids failures on mixed solid-shell structures by iteratively projecting between optimized guidance-field level sets and reg-GWN gradient ridges.

Established an efficient, memory-saving, GPU-parallel coarse-to-fine global collision checking scheme for motion planning by pairing fast UDF-based candidate rejection with time-varying reg-GWN verification.

sections.heading: 1. Introduction: Printing '3D Models in the Wild' Directly
sections.summary: While multi-axis 3D printing offers many advantages like support-free fabrication, existing pipelines assume inputs are watertight solids. To fabricate models with mixed thin-shell/solid structures and non-manifold boundaries without geometry-altering manual repair, the authors propose a complementary hybrid geometric query field.
sections.details:
### The Promise of Multi-Axis 3D Printing and the Real-World Gap
Multi-axis 3D printing is an advanced manufacturing method that exploits robotic degrees of freedom to deposit material along curved surfaces. This reduces stair-stepping artifacts and increases strength by aligning toolpaths with principal stress directions. However, most existing pipelines assume that a watertight solid, such as a tetrahedral mesh, is provided upfront.

In real design workflows, this assumption rarely holds. Geometries from CAD, digital content creation, topology optimization, or 3D scanning routinely contain zero-thickness open surfaces (thin shells) mixed with closed volumes (solids), as well as self-intersections. Feeding these into traditional multi-axis slicers requires grueling manual geometry repair using offsets or boolean operations to forcibly convert them into closed solids. Moreover, thickening thin sheets can cause adjacent surfaces to fuse unintentionally, destroying the designer's original intent.

### Limitations of Single Geometric Representations
To compute toolpaths directly without modifying geometry, one needs a differentiable representation that can query surface distance, direction, and inside/outside status from any point in space. Yet, existing single representations each have clear trade-offs:

- **Signed Distance Fields (SDF)**: While they provide clean distance and inside/outside queries, they can only be applied to strictly defined, closed solid volumes.
- **Unsigned Distance Fields (UDF)**: They can represent open surfaces and non-manifold geometries, but they lack inside/outside discrimination, and their gradients become unstable near the surface, causing boundary ambiguity.
- **Generalized Winding Numbers (GWN)**: They compute inside/outside membership even on imperfect point clouds, but lack the absolute metric distance required for collision avoidance and cannot identify precise surface locations on open sheets alone.

### The WildFab Insight
The authors observed that forcing a single representation to do everything is the root of the problem. They propose a 'hybrid query field' that fuses a neural UDF (superior for smooth spatial distance and direction queries) with a regularized GWN (reg-GWN, which provides reliable inside/outside information and sharp boundary responses). This forms the core insight behind WildFab.

sections.heading: 2. Related Work: How Prior Methods Approached the Problem and Where They Hit Limits
sections.summary: Prior work spanning 3D printing from imperfect geometries, geometric computation for multi-axis printing, and neural implicit fields with winding numbers is surveyed. Planar slicing techniques and single implicit representations cannot satisfy the spatial toolpath generation and dynamic collision avoidance requirements of multi-axis printing.
sections.details:
### 3D Printing for Imperfect Models
In traditional 3D printing, repairing broken meshes via voxelization or manifold reconstruction prior to slicing has been standard practice. Recently, generalized winding numbers (GWN) and inside/outside testing algorithms have enabled direct planar slicing of broken point clouds and thin walls, even appearing in commercial slicers. However, these methods compute planar contour intersections on horizontal cutting planes. They cannot be directly applied to multi-axis printing, which demands precise nearest-point surface projections and spatial clearance queries from arbitrary points in space.

### Geometric Computing in Multi-Axis 3D Printing
In multi-axis printing, curved layer slicing, stress-aligned toolpaths, and collision-aware trajectory generation have been actively researched. Advanced frameworks have recently introduced neural fields to optimize toolpaths and robot poses in continuous space. However, because they fundamentally rely on neural SDFs, representing self-intersecting or open-surface models without artifacts remains difficult.

### Neural UDFs and Regularized Generalized Winding Numbers (GWN)
Neural UDFs have gained traction in 3D reconstruction due to their ability to represent open surfaces. However, because neural networks have finite spectral capacity, distance values float above zero near the surface, and gradients become erratic. This leads to well-known 'near-surface ambiguity,' such as fragmented or doubled iso-surfaces.

On the other hand, while the GWN is powerful for inside/outside classification on imperfect geometric data, its standard formulation contains singularities (division by zero) on the surface, preventing differentiable cross-surface optimization. Applying a smooth regularizing kernel yields reg-GWN, which stabilizes boundary responses but does not provide absolute metric distances. Prior to this work, combining the strengths of both representations to tackle multi-axis printing challenges had not been explored.

sections.heading: 3. Geometric Representation: A Hybrid Field Combining the Best of UDFs and Winding Numbers
sections.summary: A hybrid representation is defined by complementarily coupling a neural UDF with a regularized GWN (reg-GWN). By tracking along the negative UDF gradient to find the maximum ridge of the reg-GWN gradient magnitude, surface boundaries can be localized with roughly two orders of magnitude higher accuracy than using UDFs alone.
sections.details:
### 3.1 Preliminaries: Complementary Properties of Neural UDF and reg-GWN
A neural UDF $f_{\mathrm{udf}}(\mathbf{x})$ returns the non-negative shortest distance from a point $\mathbf{x}$ to the surface. However, when trained with a finite-bandwidth network, its values float above zero near the boundary, leading to doubled or disconnected contours if one naively extracts the zero iso-surface.

Meanwhile, the generalized winding number (GWN) computes inside/outside membership through Poisson kernel integration, but suffers from singularities on the boundary surface. In this work, the authors adopt a regularized GWN (reg-GWN), $w_\delta(\mathbf{x})$, using an error-function-based regularizer $s(t)$. This eliminates singularities and transforms the discontinuous step transition across the boundary into a smooth transition layer. Computing the gradient magnitude $\|\nabla w_\delta\|$ in this transition zone produces a sharp peak—a ridge—precisely at the object's boundary surface.

### 3.2 High-Precision Boundary Detection via the Hybrid Query Field
Leveraging these properties, the authors represent the model as a hybrid query field $\mathcal{Q}(\mathbf{x}) = (f_{\mathrm{udf}}(\mathbf{x}), w_\delta(\mathbf{x}))$.

When identifying the surface boundary $\mathcal{S}$, reg-GWN alone does not indicate which spatial direction leads to the surface. The UDF gradient $-\nabla f_{\mathrm{udf}}$—a stable vector pointing perpendicular to the surface—is used as the search direction. Specifically, by moving along $-\nabla f_{\mathrm{udf}}$ and locating where the reg-GWN gradient norm $\|\nabla w_\delta\|$ reaches its local maximum, the true surface boundary is defined.

This clever combination reduces surface localization error by a factor of 50 to 100 compared to tracing UDF iso-surfaces alone. It captures sharp, accurate boundaries even along the open edges of thin sheets.

captions.F2: Comparison of query characteristics between UDF and reg-GWN. (a) For an open triangle input, UDF provides smooth spatial distances everywhere. (b) reg-GWN captures inside/outside membership. (c, d) Near-surface distance errors show large errors for UDF alone, whereas combining it with reg-GWN reduces errors by a factor of 50. (e, f) UDF gradient norms fluctuate near the surface, while the reg-GWN gradient norm produces a sharp peak upon crossing the surface.
captions.F3: Comparison of boundary detection methods. (a) UDF iso-surface extraction and gradient tracing cause doubled or disconnected contours, while the GWN 0.5 iso-surface forcibly closes open surfaces into loops. (b) Tracing the peak of the reg-GWN gradient norm along the negative UDF gradient direction enables (c) extracting accurate boundaries on open geometries with approximately two orders of magnitude higher precision.

sections.heading: 4. Multi-Axis 3D Printing: Support-Free Toolpaths and Coarse-to-Fine Collision Avoidance
sections.summary: Built on the hybrid field, a spatial toolpath generation method is developed using guidance field optimization and alternating projections. Furthermore, to eliminate nozzle collisions with the printed geometry on the GPU quickly and reliably, a coarse-to-fine collision checking scheme is proposed that pairs rapid UDF rejection with exact time-varying reg-GWN verification.
sections.details:
### 4.1 Overall Computational Pipeline
The pipeline consists of two main phases. First, the input model is converted into an oriented point cloud to construct the hybrid query field $\mathcal{Q}$, which is used to generate spatial toolpaths. Next, nozzle orientations are optimized along the print sequence to completely avoid collisions with the dynamically growing printed geometry.

### 4.2 Spatial Toolpath Generation via Latent Fields
To generate spatial toolpaths, a scalar 'guidance field' $g(\mathbf{x})$ that defines local build directions across space is optimized using a neural network. The loss function incorporates three terms:

- **Support-Free Loss ($\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{SF}}$)**: Enforces that overhang angles do not exceed a critical threshold (set to $45^\circ$).
- **Boundary Protection Loss ($\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{BP}}$)**: Constrains iso-surfaces to align parallel along open boundary loops—like the tips of Christmas tree branches—preventing toolpaths from disconnecting at thin sheet edges.
- **Smoothness Regularization ($\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{smooth}}$)**: Prevents abrupt layer thickness variations and local gouging.

After optimization, the toolpath for each layer is defined by the intersection curve between the guidance field's iso-surface and the reg-GWN gradient ridge surface. To compute this, a two-stage iterative projection is executed: candidate points filtered by UDF are projected onto the guidance field's iso-surface via Newton iterations, and then pulled back onto the reg-GWN ridge using a 1D line search along the UDF gradient direction. Fully parallelized on the GPU, over 100,000 waypoints are accurately extracted in less than 10 seconds.

### 4.3 Coarse-to-Fine Collision-Free Motion Planning via Hybrid Fields
Once toolpaths are obtained, nozzle orientations (quaternion field $\mathbf{q}$) at each waypoint are optimized to prevent collisions with previously deposited material. However, performing naive collision checks against dynamically growing shapes across tens of thousands of path points would overwhelm GPU memory.

The authors address this with a coarse-to-fine, two-stage checking strategy. Modeling the nozzle envelope as a set of line segments, the global UDF first rapidly rejects line segments that are clearly collision-free (over 99.5% of segments). For the remaining gray-zone segments, an exact ridge-intersection test is conducted using a time-varying reg-GWN ($w_{\delta\text{-TV}}$) built only from points deposited up to that timestamp. The time-varying reg-GWN successfully resolves UDF false positives (incorrect collision alarms near distance singularities), enabling fast convergence to safe, collision-free printing trajectories without erratic posture swings.

captions.F5: Overall flow of the proposed pipeline. A hybrid query field is constructed from the input model, and spatial toolpaths are generated via iterative projections between the optimized guidance field and boundary ridges. Subsequently, global collision-free multi-axis motions are produced through coarse-to-fine collision checking combining fast UDF rejection and time-varying reg-GWN verification.
captions.F7: Mechanism of coarse-to-fine collision checking. (a) Checking via UDF gradients alone produces false positives near singularities or unprinted regions, but pairing it with time-varying reg-GWN ridge responses accurately isolates true collisions. (b, c) This allows rapid convergence to collision-free nozzle poses while preserving support-free conditions.

sections.heading: 5. Experiments and Results: Robustness and Robotic Fabrication Validation
sections.summary: High-precision toolpath generation was validated on diverse inputs, including self-intersecting surfaces, topology-optimization voxels, 3D scanned point clouds, and broken Thingi10K meshes. Real-world fabrication using an 8-DoF robotic setup and micro-CT inspection confirmed artifact-free internal structures, and extensions to planar slicing and robotic welding were demonstrated.
sections.details:
### 5.1 Computational Results Across Diverse Inputs
WildFab handled a variety of 'in-the-wild' geometries that cause existing pipelines to fail:

- **Parametric Surfaces**: On 'ArtShell' and the 'Klein Bottle'—which combine self-intersections, thin sheets, and solids—the method generated continuous paths without interruption at intersection curves. For ArtShell, an initial 17% collision region was cleared in just 5 iterations (under 4 seconds per iteration), raising the support-free ratio from 92.1% to 99.2%.
- **Neural Implicit Models**: Direct integration with a latent-code decoder outputting garment UDFs produced support-free paths with protected sleeve and collar boundaries without extracting an explicit mesh.
- **Scanned Point Clouds**: Using raw, uncleaned point clouds of a statue with a thin veil ('Goddess'), the method satisfied overhang limits while preserving nested thin-sheet and solid structures.
- **Topology-Optimization Voxels**: On the 'TO-Kitten' model, outer shells and coarse internal infill were generated simultaneously without placing support structures inside inaccessible cavities.
- **Imperfect Meshes from Thingi10K**: Across 20 challenging meshes with non-manifold edges and holes where conventional planar slicing achieved support-free ratios of only 25% to 95%, WildFab achieved near-100% support-free ratios on almost every model.

### 5.2 Implementation Details and Runtimes
Experiments were conducted on an Intel Core i9-14900K with an NVIDIA RTX 4090. About 70% of total computation time was spent training the neural UDF. Once trained, generating over 100,000 waypoints took less than 10 seconds. An octree-accelerated reg-GWN queried in under 20ms, allowing collision checking loops to run efficiently.

### 5.3 Physical Robotic Fabrication Validation
Physical printing was conducted on an 8-DoF setup combining a 6-axis ABB robotic arm and a 2-axis tilt-rotary table. Thin ribbon structures on a Christmas tree and self-intersecting loops on the ArtShell were printed support-free. Scanning the fabricated parts with micro-CT (140 $\mu\mathrm{m}$ resolution) revealed an average geometric deviation of about $0.7\,\mathrm{mm}$ (approximately 0.5% of overall model size) across both inner and outer structures, confirming high geometric fidelity.

### 5.4 Applications and Parameter Analysis
The method extends naturally to planar slicing. On nested shell structures (onion skin and flesh) and clothed human digital characters—where commercial slicers accidentally fill voids—the method achieved intended multi-material, thin-shell separation. It also transfers directly to robot welding trajectory planning for non-manifold lattices like rocket grid fins.

Parameter experiments revealed an optimal regularizer width of $\delta = h / 2.5$ relative to sample point spacing $h$, balancing ridge peak damping from over-smoothing against numerical overshoot near singularities.

captions.F8: Validation on the ArtShell model containing complex self-intersections. (a) Boundary localization via the hybrid field, (b) improved distribution of support-free angles, (c) convergence to zero collisions within a few iterations, (d) nozzle orientation optimization smoothly layering across intersecting regions, and (e) the resulting physical robotic print.

sections.heading: 6. Conclusion: Freeing CAD/CAM from 'Mesh Repair Hell'
sections.summary: WildFab introduces an end-to-end framework for multi-axis 3D printing from un-repaired models in the wild by fusing neural UDFs and regularized GWN. Precise spatial toolpath generation and coarse-to-fine collision checking bridge design and robotic manufacturing directly, establishing a new geometric foundation for digital fabrication.
sections.details:
WildFab is a framework that directly generates support-free spatial toolpaths and global collision-free motions from 'models in the wild'—containing mixed thin shells and solids, self-intersections, and imperfect boundaries—without manual geometry repair.

At its core is the 'hybrid query field' concept, pairing the smooth distance queries of neural UDFs with the boundary localization power of the regularized generalized winding number (reg-GWN). This enables sub-millimeter toolpath placement in geometrically delicate regions while computing safe robot trajectories for dynamically growing shapes without exhausting GPU resources.

The framework demonstrates versatile utility beyond robotic 3D printing, transferring directly to planar multi-material slicing and robotic welding. By enabling designers and engineers to materialize unconstrained shapes directly without wrestling with mesh defects, this work represents a major step forward for CAD/CAM software and digital fabrication.

sections.heading: Appendix: Loss Formulation, Kernel Differentiability, and Quantitative Comparisons
sections.summary: The appendix details UDF training losses (including thermal diffusion regularization against ghost geometry), provides mathematical proofs for singularity removal and analytical gradients in reg-GWN, and presents quantitative comparisons against standalone neural UDF baselines like CAP-UDF.
sections.details:
### UDF Training Loss Formulation (Appendix A)
The neural UDF is trained using a SIREN architecture with a $\mathrm{softplus}$ output activation to guarantee non-negative values. In addition to on-surface zero constraints and the Eikonal loss (constraining gradient norm to 1), a boundary loss is introduced to prevent artificial capping membranes from bridging open boundary loops $\mathcal{C}$. A heat-kernel-inspired thermal diffusion regularization term is also added to suppress high-frequency 'ghost geometry' in free space.

### Singularity Removal and Differentiability of the Regularized Poisson Kernel (Appendix B)
In standard GWN, the kernel diverges when query points coincide with surface points. The authors employ a Poisson kernel $P_\delta$ regularized by an error-function-based factor $s(t) = \operatorname{erf}(t) - \frac{2t}{\sqrt{\pi}}e^{-t^2}$. Taylor expansion proves that $P_\delta \to 0$ as $\mathbf{x} \to \mathbf{p}$, completely eliminating boundary singularities. This ensures that the spatial gradient $\nabla w_\delta$ is analytically differentiable, mathematically guaranteeing sharp boundary ridge extraction.

### Quantitative Evaluation and Ablation (Appendix C)
Comparisons against pure neural UDF baselines like CAP-UDF show that UDFs alone locally smooth out tiny protrusions and sharp corners (such as screws or the Lucy statue) and accumulate distance errors. The proposed hybrid representation combining reg-GWN significantly outperforms baselines across Chamfer Distance, Hausdorff Distance, and F-score, confirming high-fidelity reproduction of fine details.

takeaways: The complementary pairing—'UDF provides the spatial search direction, while reg-GWN gradient peaks pinpoint the true boundary'—delivers a decisive breakthrough for processing imperfect geometry.
Iteratively projecting between guidance field iso-surfaces and reg-GWN boundary ridges enables reliable, high-precision toolpath extraction even on mixed non-manifold and thin-sheet models.

Dividing collision checks into '99.5% fast candidate rejection via UDF' and 'exact verification via time-varying reg-GWN' dramatically reduces computation time and GPU memory during dynamic multi-axis printing.
Eliminating manual mesh repair and forced solidifications unlocks true end-to-end digital fabrication, preserving the designer's intended open surfaces and self-intersecting features directly.
limitations: On extremely sharp edges or ultra-fine micro-features, neural UDF training exhibits slight local smoothing, meaning zero geometric loss against the input cannot be strictly guaranteed.
Neural UDF pre-training accounts for roughly 70% of total computation time; reducing training duration remains necessary for interactive, real-time printing workflows.
When estimating and propagating normals from point clouds, severe scan noise can cause local normal flips that degrade the accuracy of reg-GWN responses.
